edges.description: Focal spinal cord inflammation involves perivascular and intraparenchymal recruitment of immune cells into the lesion.
Contiguous spinal cord inflammation spanning three or more vertebral segments manifests radiologically and clinically as longitudinally extensive transverse myelitis.
Acute focal spinal cord and meningeal inflammation frequently produces localized low back pain at symptom onset.
Focal spinal cord inflammation disrupts descending and sacral autonomic pathways governing bladder control, causing neurogenic bladder dysfunction.
Focal spinal cord inflammation interrupts spinal autonomic pathways regulating bowel function, resulting in bowel dysfunction and incontinence.
Perivascular and intraparenchymal inflammatory infiltrates precede disruption of the blood-brain barrier.
Barrier breakdown permits inflammatory injury that converges on myelin and neuronal damage in the spinal cord.
Demyelination and axonal injury in descending corticospinal motor tracts impair motor conduction below the spinal lesion, producing acute muscle weakness.
Demyelination and neuronal injury across ascending sensory tracts cause numbness, paresthesias, and a truncal sensory level.
Severe bilateral corticospinal tract demyelination and axonal degeneration at peak spinal cord injury result in complete paraplegia.
Ephaptic transmission and hyperexcitability across demyelinated spinal axons generate paroxysmal painful tonic spasms.
Demyelination and neuronal injury disrupting spinal sensorimotor circuits produce secondary spinal focal dystonia.
Aberrant cellular and humoral immune responses directed against spinal cord targets drive focal spinal cord inflammation.

evidence.reference_title: Spinal movement disorders in NMOSD, MOGAD, and idiopathic transverse myelitis: a prospective observational study.
evidence.snippet: The most frequent spinal movement disorders were tonic spasms (57%), focal dystonia (25%), spinal tremor (16%), spontaneous clonus (9.5%), secondary restless limb syndrome (9.5%), and spinal myoclonus (8%).

evidence.reference_title: Predictors of recurrence following an initial episode of transverse myelitis.
evidence.snippet: Multiple independent risk factors for recurrence were identified: African American race (risk ratio 1.60, p < 0.001, 95% confidence interval 1.26-2.03; similarly noted hereafter), female sex (1.88, p = 0.007, 1.19-2.98), longitudinally extensive myelitis at onset (1.34, p = 0.036, 1.01-1.78), Sjogren syndrome antigen A (1.89, p = 0.003, 1.44-2.48), vitamin D insufficiency (4.00, p < 0.001, 1.60-10.0), antinuclear antibody titer ≥1:160 (1.69, p = 0.006, 1.23-2.32), and the presence of inflammatory markers (e.g., immunoglobulin G index) in the CSF (2.14, p < 0.001, 1.44-3.17).
